A former student of a different vocational institute (IEK) complained that the institute, run by the controller, sent him a promotional email without his consent and ignored his access and erasure request. The controller said he had left his email himself, that one employee sent the message by mistake, and that his data was deleted after his objection. The Authority found breaches of the principles of purpose limitation, lawfulness and transparency, and of the rights of access and erasure (no reply to the data subject, no valid opt-out address). It imposed a fine of EUR 5,000.

A data subject asked the company Kariera A.E. repeatedly to stop sending him job-advertisement emails and was told his data had been deleted, yet he kept receiving them. The company's Master Data Table sync failed because of a technical error that left a duplicate email record in its e-mail database. The Authority found that the company had not delivered the erasure and objection requests and lacked effective procedures to ensure erasure, breaching Article 17 with Article 21 and Article 25(1) GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 5,000.

The CNPD restricted formation investigated video surveillance at Société A, a Luxembourg company in the ABCD group, after an on-site visit in September 2019. Cameras at two sites captured parts of the public road and neighbouring land, and footage was kept for three months rather than the roughly 30 days needed. The company blurred the cameras and cut retention to 30 days after the visit, before the decision. The CNPD fined the company EUR 1,900 for breaches of Article 5(1)(c) and (e) GDPR and ordered no corrective measures because the company had already complied.

The Luxembourg CNPD investigated a company (Société A) within a four-company group after an on-site visit in September 2019 that found video surveillance in place. The restricted formation found that a camera filming the staff canteen terrace was disproportionate under the data minimisation principle, Article 5(1)(c) GDPR. The company had already masked the camera's view by the time of the decision, and the restricted formation considered the breach non-intentional and the company cooperative. It imposed a fine of EUR 2,400, lower than the EUR 2,900 proposed by the investigator, and found no breach for cameras filming a private plot the public could cross.

The CNPD's restricted formation investigated Société A, a Luxembourg company, after an on-site visit in March 2019. It found that a camera covered part of the staff canteen, so employees were watched during their breaks, and that video footage was kept longer than needed. It also found that the information given to staff and third parties about the video surveillance did not meet Article 13 GDPR. The CNPD imposed a fine of EUR 2,600 and ordered no corrective measures, because the company had already changed its system after the inspection.

The CNPD's restricted formation examined a Luxembourg company's video surveillance system (fourteen cameras, twelve working) after an on-site visit on 22 March 2019. It found that one camera captured part of a public road, breaching data minimisation under Article 5(1)(c) GDPR, and that information given to non-employee third parties (customers, suppliers, service providers, visitors) did not meet Article 13 GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 1,000 and ordered the company to bring its information notices into compliance within two months. The company's later changes were taken into account and two other proposed corrective measures were not imposed.

The Portuguese data protection authority (CNPD) warned a university that using two remote-exam applications together, Respondus Lockdown Browser and Respondus Monitor, is liable to infringe the principles of lawfulness, purpose limitation, data minimisation and proportionality (Art. 5(1)(a), (b) and (c) GDPR). The online exams had not started, so no personal data had yet been processed in that setting, but the applications were already available for installation and students had been encouraged to try them, so the American processor, Respondus, Inc., had probably already received some data. The CNPD also found that students' and staff members' personal data cannot be sent to the US on the basis of standard contractual clauses without effective supplementary measures (the Schrems II judgment). It ordered the university to have the processor delete at once any personal data collected when students installed the applications, with a written record of the deletion. The operative part is a warning about the planned processing (Art. 58(2)(a)), not a finding that a breach had already happened. It imposed no fine. The reasoning also examines Art. 6(1)(f) (legitimate interests, rejected) and Art. 22 (automated decisions); the warning itself names Art. 5(1)(a) to (c). Approved on 11 May 2021.

The Hamburg DPA (HmbBfDI) issued an order under the GDPR's urgency procedure prohibiting Facebook Ireland Ltd. from processing personal data from WhatsApp for its own purposes. The order is immediately enforceable.

Tested.Me Ltd, a provider of digital track-and-trace services, sent two marketing emails promoting its Digital Health Passport App to about 84,000 people who had ticked a marketing box on a venue visitor registration form. The Commissioner found that the consent relied on was not informed, specific or freely given, so the emails breached Regulation 22 of PECR. The company was fined £8,000, reduced to £6,400 if paid early.
The Slovenian DPA (IP) held that an eGovernment portal had violated Article 32 of the GDPR by failing to ensure that documents posted on its bulletin adequately secured personal data.

The Romanian authority closed an investigation in April 2021 into World Class România S.A. after receiving a complaint. The company had posted an employee's resignation request in the staff WhatsApp group, exposing the employee's name, address, ID details and personal numeric code to all group members. The authority found that Article 32 GDPR was breached because the technical and organisational measures were insufficient. It imposed a fine of 9,851.00 lei (about EUR 2,000) and ordered the company to implement appropriate measures for remote transmission of personal data, including regular staff training, within 30 days.

A policyholder complained that his health data and other data obtained through a hospitalisation insurance were used for other purposes and passed to third parties listed in the insurer's privacy statement, without a choice. The Litigation Chamber had fined the insurer EUR 50,000 in decision 24/2020, but the Market Court annulled it because the insurer had not been able to defend itself fully. In this reconsideration the Chamber again found breaches of the lawfulness and transparency principles, the accountability duty and the information duties (Arts 5, 6, 12, 13), including lack of a demonstrated legitimate interest for staff training and CCTV storage. It reduced the fine to EUR 30,000, as the Article 6 breach covers only two purposes and the insurer had already revised its privacy statement.

The Romanian DPA concluded an investigation on 6 May 2021 into a homeowners' association in Iași, triggered by a complaint about posting payment lists with members' full names and a defamatory notice containing the complainant's name. The association did not answer the authority's information requests, although it confirmed receiving them. It was fined RON 2,463.3 (about EUR 500) and ordered to send all requested information within 5 working days of receiving the report.

The Norwegian DPA (Datatilsynet) fined the Norwegian Olympic and Paralympic Committee and Confederation of Sports (NIF) about €123,656 (NOK 1,250,000) for a data breach in which the personal data of 3.2 million people was exposed online.

The Norwegian DPA published a draft decision notifying Disqus that it will be fined approximately €2.5 million (NOK 25 000 000) for unlawfully processing personal data for programmatic advertising purposes. In addition, the DPA found that Disqus breached transparency and information requirements by not providing data subjects with adequate information about the company's tracking, profiling and disclosure of personal data.

The Spanish DPA fined an energy company €1,500,000 for not providing sufficient information to data subjects under Article 13 GDPR, and for not implementing adequate measures to avoid or mitigate risks related to the data processing under Article 25 GDPR.

The Spanish DPA fined an energy company €1,500,000 for not providing sufficient information to data subjects under Article 13 GDPR, and for not implementing adequate measures to avoid or mitigate risks related to the data processing under Article 25 GDPR.

The Austrian data protection authority found that neither the GDPR nor the Austrian law implementing the GDPR will apply to the transfer of health data between two individuals via WhatsApp, as such processing fall's under the GDPR's household exemption.

The EDPS found that the CJEU had breached data protection requirements in relation to web tracking. They were found to have insufficient information on their site, and a banner which did not allow users to reject cookies.

Following their decision to fine Google €100,000,000 for not complying with the cookies regulation, the CNIL accepted Google's adjustments and decided to close the case. However, the DPA stated that this only refers to the precautionary measures taken in their original decision, and reserved the right to further analyze Google compliance with the cookies regulation and the latest CNIL guidelines on the matter.

After a complaint, the Garante found that the municipality of Santa Ninfa had published on its website a council resolution that named the complainant and set out details of enforcement-related payment notices. The document stayed freely downloadable for almost a year, well beyond the 15-day period for the online notice board. The municipality said the publication was an unintended error caused by a software-house update, and it removed the document after the Authority's request. The Garante found breaches of GDPR Articles 5(1)(a) and (c), 6(1)(c) and (e), 6(2) and 6(3)(b), and Article 2-ter of the Italian Privacy Code. It imposed a single fine of EUR 2,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

InfoMentor, which develops and runs the Mentor school information system, reported a personal data breach in February 2019. A logged-in parent exploited a flaw in which a pupil's system number in the URL exposed national identification numbers and avatars, affecting 423 children in Iceland and one child in Sweden. The Authority found that InfoMentor failed to ensure adequate security under Art. 32(1)(b) and (d) GDPR, and that it breached Art. 5(1)(f) by sending pupils' identification numbers to the wrong schools. It imposed an administrative fine of ISK 3,500,000 and ordered InfoMentor to implement procedures for breach response and security testing.

The Icelandic DPA held that a police officer had not violated the law on the processing of personal data for law enforcement purposes, by refusing an access request to personal data registered in the Schengen Information System (SIS).

A complaint was filed against a bank for passing a customer's data to a company without consent. The data protection authority sent the company three requests for explanations, but the company never collected any of the letters, so they were deemed delivered. The authority opened a separate procedure and found that the company breached the duty to cooperate and to give the authority access to necessary information. It imposed a fine of PLN 22,739 (equivalent to EUR 5,000), taking the failure to give access to information as the most serious breach.

A dispatcher complained that a phone call made on duty was recorded without his consent or information by a transport organiser (Company 1). The recording was then passed to his employer (Company 2), which used it to investigate him and start the end of his employment. The authority partly upheld the complaint and found that both companies lacked a valid legal basis and did not give proper transparent information. It ordered both to fix their practice. It fined Company 1 HUF 500,000 and Company 2 HUF 200,000, and awarded the complainant HUF 10,000 for the authority's missed deadline. The other parts of the complaint were rejected.

A woman learned that her credit file at the National Bank of Belgium's consumer credit register had been consulted 20 times between 2016 and 2018 by a financial company, where her ex-husband worked as a manager. He admitted the abusive consultations. The Litigation Chamber found that the company had no adequate security measures governing managers' access to the register, and also found a breach of the right of access (Article 15). It ordered the company to bring managers' access into compliance within three months and imposed an administrative fine of EUR 100,000.

The Spanish DPA fined Equifax, a credit ranking agency, €1,000,000 for failing to comply with Article 5(1)(a), 5(1)(b), 5(1)(c), 5(1)(d) and with Article 14 GDPR. The authority ordered Equifax to stop the processing and to delete the related database.

A press release dated 13 May 2021 reports that ANSPDCP closed an investigation of Telekom Romania Communications SA on 23 April 2021. A former customer had withdrawn consent and later objected to marketing, yet was phoned again for marketing by a Telekom representative, whom the company said acted through human error. The authority found processing without a legal basis (Art. 6) and disregard of the right to object (Art. 21). Telekom received a warning for Art. 6 and a fine of 9,851.40 lei (about EUR 2,000) for Art. 21.

The Italian DPA issued a general warning on 23 April 2021 about the processing of personal data under decree-law no. 52 of 22 April 2021, which introduced the national Covid-19 'green certificate'. It found that the decree may breach GDPR Articles 5, 6(3)(b), 9, 13, 14, 25 and 32, citing lack of prior consultation, unclear purposes and legal basis, data minimisation, accuracy, transparency, retention and security. The Garante warned the Ministries and the Conference of the Regions, ordered publication in the Official Gazette, and sent a copy to the Prime Minister.

The Italian DPA found that the disclosure of certain databases regarding COVID-19 by schools in the Province of Modena may enable the identification of pupils and their health status, even where data which directly identifies the pupils is removed.

A complainant objected to a family allowance fund (an ASBL, a non-profit, that the decision calls Y2) consulting the national register history of household composition for his adult son's file, which also showed the complainant as a former household head. The Chamber Contentieuse found that the full, unlimited history was disproportionate and that the fund had no valid legal basis under Article 6, which also breached the data minimisation principle (Article 5(1)(c)). It also found breaches of Articles 24 and 5(2) for the fund's accountability failure, and a later consultation during the proceedings was also held unlawful. The sanction was a reprimand against the fund.

The Belgian DPA held that in this specific case, concerning a father and mother sharing parental authority, the request to have data about the child erased, introduced by the father alone, had not been submitted in a way that could be accepted. The Belgian DPA also found several other violations of the GDPR by the controller.

The Polish DPA fined a satellite platform operator €250,000 for violating Article 24(1),Article 32(1), and Article 32(2) GDPR for not implementing appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the security of personal data when cooperating with a courier company. See comment.
The Luxembourg DPA issued a warning to a controller that had not adequately informed its employees about a geolocation system used in its company vehicles.

The Sanctions Board of the Finnish Data Protection Ombudsman's Office fined ParkkiPate Oy, a parking-enforcement company, EUR 75,000. Between 2017 and 2020 individuals complained that the company had not granted access to their data or erased it, and that it demanded excessive identifying information (personal identity number, address, a standard form) before handling requests and complaints. The Board found breaches of the GDPR's data protection principles and of data subjects' rights (Articles 12 to 22). It treated the breach of Article 15 as the most serious and counted the company's abandonment of the identity-number requirement as a mitigating factor.

A data subject complained in February 2020 about the online booking form for follow-up visits at the Tor Vergata hospital foundation, which collected health-related data over unencrypted http and without the Article 13 information. The Garante found breaches of the integrity and confidentiality and transparency principles and of Articles 13, 25 and 32. No corrective measures were ordered because the hospital had meanwhile switched to https and provided the information. It imposed a fine of EUR 15,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Spanish DPA found that an impact study carried out by the Spanish Government on daily commuting trends during the COVID-19 pandemic was carried out in compliance with the GDPR, since the Government had implemented appropriate measures to prevent data misuse.

The Hungarian authority opened an own-initiative proceeding against a company after a complaint-based investigation could not clarify the facts. The company had claimed it had no website and processed no personal data, but a domain registrar confirmed it used a website that collected names, e-mails and phone numbers via a contact form. The company ignored all of the authority's orders, including a procedural fine, and so could not demonstrate GDPR compliance. The authority found breaches of Articles 5(2) and 24 GDPR and imposed a fine of HUF 1,000,000.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in March 2021 into Lugera & Makler Broker S.R.L., a processor acting for Raiffeisen Bank SA. An employee sales agent carried out 1,372 pre-scoring checks and destroyed the original documents instead of handing them over to the bank, which caused a security incident affecting 1,058 people. The company had not ensured that persons acting under its authority process data only on instruction, and had not put adequate technical and organisational security measures in place. It was fined 7,331.85 lei (about EUR 1,500) for breaching Articles 29 and 32(2) and (4) GDPR.

A neighbour complained that cameras installed at a bar with a terrace were aimed at public space without authorisation. The AEPD found that the cameras captured an excessive part of the public pavement, neighbouring buildings and parked cars without justification, and that the posted sign did not identify the controller. The operative part finds an infringement of Article 5(1)(c) GDPR and imposes a fine of EUR 1,500 on the individual operating the bar, described as the lowest band for this type of infringement.

A candidate in municipal elections sent promotional SMS messages to a complainant's mobile phone, though the complainant had no prior relationship with him. The candidate could not show prior consent, had no procedure ensuring consent was obtained, and gave no easy way to object in the message. The Authority found breaches of Article 11 of Law 3471/2006 and imposed a fine of EUR 2,000. The text is the corrected re-issue of decision 8/2021 (marked as a repeat corrected for an error in the panel's composition); the document carries the date 16 April 2021, and the Authority examined the case in its session of 2 December 2020. A first issue of the same decision, dated 22 March 2021, is also on the Authority's website.

A complainant's employer-side municipality emailed the complainant's trade union to ask whether it funded courses she had taken, attaching her receipts. The union replied with the courses she had already been paid for in full, including dates and amounts. Persónuvernd found that neither the municipality nor the union had a legal basis under the Icelandic Data Protection Act and Article 6 GDPR for this disclosure, so the processing did not comply with the law. No fine or order is stated in the text.

The Romanian DPA investigated a food company after a complaint that it filmed employees with cameras in offices, changing rooms and the canteen. It found excessive video monitoring of employees in changing rooms and the dining area, justified by protecting goods and deterring theft, which could be achieved with less intrusive means. Consent in an employer-employee relationship was not freely given and no other legal basis was found. The company was fined RON 24,362.50 (equivalent to EUR 5,000) and ordered to bring video monitoring into line with data minimisation and to reorient camera angles.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined a landlord €3000 for violating Articles 5(1)(c) and 13 GDPR in relation to a video surveillance system in an apartment building.

A local health authority notified the Garante of a breach: a doctor's conference slides on a clinical case, containing a patient's initials, age, detailed history, dates and 22 photographs, were published on the website of the Triveneto surgery society after winning a best clinical case prize. The patient was identifiable and had not consented. The Garante found the publication amounted to prohibited dissemination of health data in breach of Articles 5(1)(a) and (c), 6 and 9 GDPR and Article 2-septies(8) of the Italian Code. It fined the society EUR 2,000, taking into account its prompt removal and de-indexing, its voluntary non-profit nature and the small number of likely viewers. No corrective measures were ordered and the decision is to be published.

A hospital doctor used a patient's health data, including identifiable clinical history, diagnostic images and 22 surgical photographs, in slides for a medical congress and a 'best clinical case 2017' prize. The slides were later published on the website of a surgical society. The patient had not consented, the doctor did not seek authorisation from the health authority (the controller), and the data were not effectively anonymised. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and (c), 6 and 9 GDPR and fined the doctor EUR 5,000, with publication of the decision. No corrective measures were imposed because the slides had been removed and disciplinary proceedings had been brought against the doctor.

The Garante received a complaint that a person's data in a food-aid application filed with the City of Palermo had been accessed by an unauthorised operator of a third-sector association. The City ran a 'Centrale Unica Aiuti Alimentari' platform and gave third-sector helper organisations a single shared login per organisation, which let operators search applications by tax code (even the first three characters) and see personal and income data. The Garante found breaches of integrity and confidentiality, data protection by design and default, and security of processing. It fined the City EUR 40,000, taking into account the large number of data subjects, the roughly two-month duration and health data, against the emergency context and the City's later security measures. No further corrective measures were ordered, and the decision is to be published.

A complainant said INPS never answered two certified-email requests to its Bolzano office asking how his contribution statement had allegedly reached third parties. INPS admitted the lack of reply, blaming an email mishap, and argued the events were too old and the records no longer kept. The Garante found that INPS failed to answer the access requests within the legal time limits, breaching Articles 5(1)(a), 12 and 15 GDPR. It fined INPS EUR 12,000 and ordered publication of the decision. It took no action on the original access to the contribution statement because of the time elapsed.

The Polish DPA held that printouts from a bank's IT system could not constitute evidence of proper communication to a data subject regarding its intention to process his personal data for the purposes of a creditworthiness assessment. In the absence of other evidence, the DPA concluded that the bank had breached its information provision obligation.
The Slovenian DPA stated that it is allowed to make public only those minutes of the parent council meetings that contain public information.
The Slovenian DPA stated that, according to the Slovenian Personal Data Protection Act, a public body could not link two medical registries without the DPA's prior permission.

The Spanish DPA decided that a controller could not require a data subject to identify themselves with their national ID, when this document had not been asked for in the first place. In this instance, the controller had no reason to doubt the identity of the data subject.

Datatilsynet fined Miljø- og Kvalitetsledelse AS, which runs a car wash, NOK 35,000 for an unlawful disclosure of camera footage. After vandalism at a payment terminal, the company sent the footage and information from its camera surveillance, unprompted, to the employer of the person it believed was responsible. The footage had already been handed to the police, so the disclosure to the employer was unnecessary, and the authority found no legal basis under Article 6(1) and the principle in Article 5(1)(a). Because the breach occurred before the GDPR applied, the fine was set according to the practice under the old law.

The Dutch DPA investigated TikTok Inc. on its own initiative and found that between 25 May 2018 and 28 July 2020 it gave its privacy policy to Dutch users, including children, only in English. This breached the duty in Article 12(1) GDPR to inform in clear and plain language, especially children. The AP rejected TikTok's arguments that the Irish authority was competent (the infringement ended before 29 July 2020) and that the rule was too vague (lex certa). It started from a base fine of EUR 525,000 and raised it to the category maximum of EUR 750,000 because of the gravity and duration, imposing a fine of EUR 750,000.

The Belgian DPA held that, for lack of a legal basis pursuant to Article 6 GDPR, a notary cannot consult the national register for natural persons in order to obtain personal data for other purposes than those defined by the law and within the scope of their profession.

The CNPD restricted formation examined geolocation of company vehicles used by employees at Société A, following an investigation it opened on its own initiative in February 2019. It found that the company kept geolocation data for 2 years and 4 months, which exceeded what was necessary (Article 5(1)(e)), and that it did not properly inform employees (Article 13). It also found a security breach under Article 32(1) for shared logins, but did not base a fine on it. The authority imposed a fine of EUR 2,800 and ordered the company to bring processing into compliance within two months.
The Slovenian DPA held that on the basis of Article 15 GDPR it is not possible for an employee to obtain information about the data processing activities of other employees within a hospital.

The Slovenian DPA held that a building manager can disclose data to a unit owner without the consent of others, if the disclosure is necessary for the proper determination of contractual obligations. This information may only be provided in a manner that precludes disclosure by unauthorised persons.

A data subject, a certified court expert, complained that a search engine operator refused his 19 March 2020 request to delist two URLs. The URLs led to an official court-expert list showing his home address, and he said he had received a death threat. The authority found that the first respondent (the search engine operator) had infringed his right to erasure by not granting the request, because the public-interest and information interests did not override his interest given the risk to his physical integrity. It ordered delisting of the two URLs within two weeks. The complaint against the second respondent, the Austrian subsidiary, was dismissed because the request had only been addressed to the first respondent.

A complainant, an employee, told the HDPA that his employer, a small partnership, had installed a camera since July 2018 that filmed his workplace and was used to monitor him rather than for security. The company said the camera was for security at the office entrance and was never used to watch staff, but the HDPA found the camera captured the whole office, including employees' workspaces, and that the owner could watch the live feed remotely by phone at any time. The HDPA held that this breached data minimisation under Article 5(1)(c) and lacked a lawful basis under Article 6(1)(f), and imposed a fine of EUR 2,000, taking into account the company's small size, the camera having been switched off, it being a first offence, and the pandemic.
The Icelandic DPA held that a primary school was not permitted to disclose information about a child to a consulting company after termination of collaboration.
The Slovenian DPA held that self-employed individuals do not enjoy protection of their personal data when operating as business entities.
The AEPD fined a controller €3000 for abandoning documentation containing personal data next to a building, which was considered a data breach and therefore a violation of Article 32(1) GDPR.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined a controller €3000 for the infringement of Article 32(1) GDPR, due to a data breach that was caused by the abandonment of several envelopes containing confidential medical data in a field.
The Spanish DPA fined Vodafone €150,000 (reduced to €90,000) for processing personal data without consent or any other legal basis.

The Swedish authority IMY, as lead supervisory authority, examined two cross-border complaints that Klarna Bank AB had not properly answered access requests under Article 15 GDPR. For complaint 1, Klarna sent the information and copy of the data only in June 2019, more than five months after the request, so IMY found a breach of Article 12(3). IMY issued a reprimand because the breach was minor. For complaint 2, IMY found the data was provided without undue delay and no violation.

The Romanian DPA published a press release saying that it had finished an investigation of Telekom Romania Mobile Communications in February 2021. It found that the company had not applied adequate technical and organisational security measures. Data of 99,210 customers, including national ID numbers, were disclosed or accessed without authorisation because wrong billing addresses went into a database passed to a debt-assignment partner. Separately, 413 customers' MyAccount data was accessed without authorisation. The company was fined the equivalent of EUR 10,000 under the GDPR, and RON 15,000 under Law 506/2004. It was also ordered to review its security measures and set up regular testing.

The Slovenian DPA stated that video surveillance performed by an individual from his private facility or from his private property to the neighbor falls under the exception of "personal use". Therefore, the DPA has no jurisdiction under the GDPR.

A staff member complained that the boarding school had published, in the 'Amministrazione Trasparente' section of its website, a contract document stating that the complainant had failed to draw up a report. The document stayed online from 18 July 2018 to 5 December 2019 and the school named no legal basis for publishing it. The Garante found the dissemination unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a) and 6 GDPR and Article 2-ter of the Code, but found no breach of Article 5(1)(c). It imposed a fine of EUR 1,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website; no further corrective measures were needed because the conduct had ended.

The Italian Garante investigated Fastweb after hundreds of complaints and reports about unwanted telemarketing calls made by Fastweb and its sales network. It found seven groups of violations: no control over the chain of data collection by sales partners, use of third-party contact lists without valid consent, defects in the 'Call me back' service, inadequate security against repeated unauthorised database access, failure to notify the resulting data breach, inaccurate data when handling data subject rights, and marketing without valid consent or a valid legitimate-interest basis. It imposed a fine of EUR 4,501,868, equal to 5% of the maximum fine (EUR 90,037,367), together with corrective orders, two processing bans and publication of the decision.

Two complainants received repeated promotional emails from OneDirect despite objecting by certified email, and their requests and the Garante's information requests went unanswered because the company's PEC mailbox was not monitored. The company could not document consent, did not produce its own record of processing activities, and cooperated poorly with the authority. The Garante found breaches of Articles 6(1)(a), 7(1), 12, 24, 30 and 31 GDPR and of the Italian Code. It banned further promotional use of data without documented consent, issued warnings, ordered organisational measures to answer data subject requests, and fined the company EUR 30,000 with publication of the decision.

A man complained that the publisher of the newspaper La Stampa had not answered his request to erase or anonymise his data in an old online archive article about a court case, and had ignored his request of 14 March 2019. The Garante found the erasure request unfounded because the archive use is compatible with the original journalistic purpose and the article had been de-indexed from search engines. It also took no action on the request to update the article, since the complainant had provided no documents on later developments. It upheld the complaint on the failure to reply to the data subject's request, rejected the 'involuntary oversight' excuse, and fined the company EUR 20,000, with publication of the decision.

A candidate in a voluntary mobility procedure complained that the municipality of Castellanza published on its website a determination containing the personal data of the participants, including home addresses, and that it could be found through search engines. The Garante found the dissemination had no adequate legal basis, since transparency legislation does not require publishing such data, and breached the lawfulness and minimisation principles. It imposed a fine of EUR 4,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website. No further corrective measures were needed because the publication had ceased.

The Hungarian authority examined the camera surveillance system (25 cameras) in a care home for elderly residents, after a complaint in 2018 and an investigation. It found that some cameras served unlawful purposes, others were unsuitable for the stated purpose, the legal basis was wrong, and information to residents and staff was inadequate. It ordered the operator to switch off or redirect the unlawful cameras, use a proper legal basis and give proper information, and imposed a fine of HUF 500,000.

A patient, through his lawyer, asked a dental implant company for a copy of his clinical file under Article 15 GDPR and got no reply within the one-month limit. The company also ignored the Garante's invitation to comply. It answered only after proceedings were opened, 182 days after the request, and sent only part of the documents, saying it held nothing more. The Garante found breaches of Articles 12(3) and 15 and fined the company EUR 7,000. It ordered publication of the decision and found no need for corrective measures because the conduct had ended.

The Italian DPA issued an urgent measure against TikTok under Articles 58(2)(d) and (f) and 66(1) GDPR. It ordered TikTok to put in place an age gate that keeps out users under 13 and under 14 who lack parental authorisation, and imposed a temporary limitation on processing the data of users whose age cannot be verified. The measure follows earlier urgency orders of 22 January and 11 February 2021 and runs until 22 April 2021. No fine is imposed; the merits proceeding was still pending.

The Slovenian Information Commissioner ran an inspection after a news website linked to a PDF of a criminal complaint that exposed the birth dates, EMŠO numbers and home addresses of named suspects, plus names of other individuals. The redaction was reversible (black boxes could be removed or the text copied), and it was still so on the second check, 25 March 2021. The Commissioner found the publisher failed to ensure security of processing under Article 32 GDPR. It ordered the data to be covered or deleted within 5 days and confirmation to be sent within 3 days after that. No fine was imposed; the decision is final in the administrative procedure, with an administrative dispute possible.

The District Office e-mailed an unprotected Excel file with detailed Covid-19 rapid test and health data of 1,153 people to all GPs in three districts, without sorting it by practice and without encryption or a password. The authority learned of it from a public-interest report by a private person. It found breaches of Article 32(1)(a)-(b) and (2), and of Articles 33(1) and 34(1), because the office did not notify the breach or inform the data subjects after a faulty risk analysis. It ordered the office to inform the data subjects within 15 days, fined it HUF 10,000,000 and ordered publication of the decision with the office's identity.
The Slovenian DPA stated that the director (CEO) or member of the management of the company shall not be a DPO.

A shareholder complained that a company capital-reduction extract, published in the Moniteur belge at his notary's request, included his payout details and bank account number, and that the publisher refused his erasure request under Article 17 GDPR. The Chambre Contentieuse found that the controller could not rely on Article 6(1)(c) or 6(1)(e) as a lawful basis for publishing those amounts and account numbers. It issued a reprimand and ordered the controller to act on the erasure request within 30 days. It did not impose a fine, because the controller is a public authority and the Chambre is not permitted to fine it.

A former member of a religious community complained that the community had breached his rights to confidentiality, access, erasure and objection after it announced his leaving in a meeting, passed his data to its administrative office, gave him an incomplete access response and refused to delete his data. The authority dismissed all four complaints. It held that membership questions, the announcement of departures and the internal record-keeping are the community's internal affairs, outside its competence. It also held that the access response was complete and that Article 15(3) GDPR gives no right to copies of whole documents. The decision is final.

The Romanian supervisory authority finished an investigation into Medicover in February 2021. The investigation began after Medicover sent several personal data breach notifications about personal and health data sent to people other than the intended recipients, by email or post. The authority found that Medicover had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure that people acting under its authority process data only on its instructions. It fined the company RON 9,749.6 (about EUR 2,000) and ordered it to review its security measures, train staff and make sure data are accurate.

The Irish DPC conducted an own-volition inquiry into Irish Credit Bureau DAC after a personal data breach in which 1,062 inaccurate accounts were shared with credit bureau members and data subjects following database coding changes. It found infringements of Articles 25(1), 5(2) and 24(1) GDPR, issued a reprimand, and imposed a fine only for the Article 25(1) infringement. The fine was set at EUR 220,000 before mitigation, reduced by EUR 130,000 for mitigating factors, giving EUR 90,000. No fine was imposed for the Articles 5(2) and 24(1) infringement.

A data subject in Spain asked Rebtel Networks AB to erase her data on 18 September 2019, but the company did not handle this as an erasure request. She kept receiving marketing emails, and the remaining data was only erased on 9 November 2020. On 22 September 2019 the company also wrongly told her that her data had been erased and that she would receive no more emails. The Swedish authority IMY found breaches of Article 17 and Article 12(3) GDPR but judged them minor and issued a reprimand instead of a fine.

A complainant received a phone call on her mobile from the office of a candidate in the July 2019 Greek national elections, asking her to vote for the candidate. The complainant said she was not a party member and asked for her data to be checked. The controller did not show that it checked national opt-out registers before the calls, did not show it informed the called person of their rights, and did not properly satisfy the complainant's access request. The Authority found breaches of Article 15 GDPR and Article 11 of Law 3471/2006 and imposed a fine of EUR 2,000. The Authority examined the case in its session of 2 December 2020; this document is dated 22 March 2021. A corrected re-issue of the same text, dated 16 April 2021, also exists (marked as a repeat corrected for an error in the panel's composition).
The Slovenian DPA decided that covert video surveillance of employees is not permissible in any manner or under any circumstances.
The Polish DPA (UODO) imposed a fine of €5000 on a company for failing to cooperate with the DPA in the investigation of a complaint about irregularities in the processing of personal data.

The Slovenian DPA decided that it is permissible for an individual to disclose to a third party the blog author's specific health information. Information whose content meets the definition of health data in point 15 of Article 4 GDPR is health information even if it is published by the person himself.

The Slovenian DPA stated that obtaining information on the child's health and developmental characteristics, knowledge of which is necessary for the child's safety and work with the child, and on whether the child has been vaccinated, is not appropriate at the stage of submitting an application for enrollment in kindergarten.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined an audit company €3,000 for a security breach occurred when they sent the claimant information of another client, instead of theirs.

A complainant objected to Creditinfo, a credit reference agency, keeping and using information about his past payment defaults, already settled, when preparing credit ratings. He also asked that processing be stopped and that he be told how the scores are calculated. The Icelandic DPA found that using the past blacklist entries was lawful under the legitimate-interests basis, in line with earlier decisions and Creditinfo's operating licence. It held that the mathematical model is outside its supervision, and that it could not order processing to stop without the data subject's consent. The processing was found compliant, so no fine or order was imposed.
The Slovenian DPA (IP) stated that, when courts process personal data as an judicial authority, the IP is not competent under Article 55(3) GDPR.

The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) ordered the defendant (a public institution) to comply with the principles of purpose limitation and data minimization, by removing the mention of the title of nobility from the identity card of the complainant.

The Bavarian DPA ("Bayrisches Landesamt für Datenschutzaufsicht" - BayLDA) held that the use of the newsletter tool Mailchimp by a German company was unlawful as Mailchimp receives email adresses of newsletter subscribers and might qualify as an "electronic communication service provider" under US surveillance law.
The AEPD fined €3,000 a Cultural Association for sharing in WeChat pictures of the minor child of the complainant without their consent.

Teachers at two lower secondary schools required pupils to download the Strava training app onto their private phones for PE lessons, and used its tracking function to check task completion. The municipality notified a personal data breach to Datatilsynet on 5 May 2020. Datatilsynet found that the municipality had no risk assessment, no DPIA and no routines for approving apps, and fined it NOK 50,000 for infringements of Articles 32(1)(b) with Article 5, 24(1) and 35 GDPR. The decision stresses that the problem was the municipality's app procedures, not Strava itself.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined Air Europa Líneas Aéreas S.A. €600,000 for the infringement of Articles 32(1) and 33 GDPR, due to the lack of appropriate technical and organisational measures and of an adequate level of security and due to the delay in the notification of a personal data breach.

Asker municipality published its mailing lists (postlister) on its website with document titles containing national ID numbers and confidential information, including about children (special education, PPT decisions, housing grants), over about 16 years. A private person alerted the municipality, which notified the Datatilsynet. The authority found there was no legal basis for publication, inadequate security ensuring confidentiality and inadequate routines for handling the lists. It imposed an administrative fine of NOK 1,000,000.

The Slovenian DPA held that the Ministry of Public Administration did not provide the relevant information under Article 13 GDPR when processing expressions of interest for COVID-19 vaccination on the e-government portal.

The Slovenian DPA decided that personal data collected when registering an interest in vaccination through the e-government portal may only be processed after the individual has received clear, accurate and reliable information about who is collecting it and for what purpose.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined Vodafone €100,000 (reduced to €60,000 for voluntary payment and acknowledgement of responsibility) for repeatedly processing of personal data of a data subject that had opposed the processing.

A complainant asked the Akureyri Hospital for copies of her and her child's medical records, but the hospital mailed them to the child's legal residence, where the child's father lives, instead of to her. The records were returned unopened by registered post and then sent to her correctly. The Data Protection Authority found that the hospital's procedures did not ensure the address was checked against the request, which fell short of the security requirements, and that this was seriously blameworthy given the sensitive health data. The processing was held to be in breach of the Icelandic data protection act, but no fine was imposed. The complaint about how the registered letter was delivered was dismissed as outside the Authority's competence.

A complainant asked the municipality of San Marco in Lamis to remove from its website two mayoral orders containing his and his family members' personal data (birth date and place, tax code, residence), linked to an unauthorised building works case. The municipality refused, and the data stayed online for more than three years, beyond the 15-day period for the public notice board, and were reachable through an archive page found by search engines. The Garante found breaches of the data minimisation principle, of the lack of a legal basis for publication beyond 15 days, and of the related GDPR principles, and imposed a fine of EUR 3,000 plus publication of the decision on its website.

The Dutch DPA received a complaint in July 2018 about sensors in Enschede's city centre that picked up the wifi signals of passers-by's phones. The investigation found that eleven sensors collected pseudonymised MAC addresses, signal strength, date and time from hundreds of thousands of people between 25 May 2018 and 30 April 2020. The municipality had no legal basis for this processing, so it breached Article 5(1)(a) in conjunction with Article 6(1) GDPR. The AP fined the municipality EUR 600,000, raising the EUR 525,000 base amount by EUR 75,000 because of the seriousness and the municipality's culpability.

The Italian DPA investigated call centre Mediacom after hundreds of complaints about unwanted telemarketing calls made for TIM. Between 2016 and 2019 Mediacom called 15,410 'referenced' numbers outside the contact lists, 11,232 of them for TIM, with no valid consent or other legal basis. The consent on the purchased lists was not specific or free, and only a sample of the lists was checked. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and 6(1), permanently restricted the processing, ordered compliance and imposed a fine of EUR 15,000, taking into account Mediacom's financial crisis after losing the TIM contract, and ordered publication of the decision.

After hundreds of complaints about unwanted promotional calls made on behalf of TIM, the Garante inspected the call centre Planet Group. It found the company called 47,981 'referenced' numbers outside TIM's lists without a legal basis or consent, kept calling people who had objected, called some people very insistently, and had inadequate privacy-by-design. The Garante treated Planet Group as de facto (joint) controller, imposed a permanent limitation of the processing with compliance orders, and fined it EUR 80,000, with publication of the decision.

A guesthouse operator, a sole trader, scanned the identity documents of foreign guests without a valid legal basis and without being able to prove consent. The operator also failed to give guests the information required by Articles 13 and 14 and to facilitate their data subject rights. The authority issued a penalty order finding two offences, fined the operator CZK 5,000 under the absorption principle, and ordered the operator to stop scanning, delete existing scans, and bring the information duties into line within 15 days.

The Baden-Württemberg data protection commissioner closed proceedings against VfB Stuttgart 1893 AG and imposed a fine of EUR 300,000 for negligent breach of the accountability obligation under Art. 5(2) GDPR. The club and its parent association cooperated extensively with the investigation. Besides the fine, the company restructured its data protection management and will support youth data protection awareness projects. Some publicly discussed matters could not be fully examined because of limitation rules. This is a press release, not the full fine notice.

The Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) fined Filigrana Comunicación with €8,000 for the infringement of Articles 6(1), 13 and 14 GDPR, as the company gathered and re-used data from the Andalusian Education Department without a legitimate basis, and they did not fulfill their information obligations.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of €50,000 to EQUIFAX IBERICA, S.L. for including the personal data of the claimant in its solvency file without legal basis for it.

A customer complained that Landsbankinn asked for the year-end balance of his account at another bank (Kvika banki) before allowing him to withdraw ISK 3 million in cash, which he said was disproportionate and unnecessary. Landsbankinn relied on its duty under the Icelandic anti-money-laundering act to verify the source of funds. Persónuvernd found the processing lawful as necessary for a legal obligation, found the data-minimisation requirement met, and rejected the complaint.

A complainant objected to Wedo ehf., the operator of the online marketplace Bland.is, looking up users' registered addresses and publishing their postcodes with listings. Wedo said it relied on consent. The DPA found the consent was not freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, and that Wedo had not assessed legitimate interests, so the processing was not lawful. The DPA ordered Wedo to stop processing users' addresses until it documents a lawful basis and the DPA confirms compliance, with confirmation due by 24 March 2021. No fine was imposed.

A debt collection firm, Lögheimtan ehf., passed a court judgment debt of a data subject to the credit information agency Creditinfo Lánstraust hf. while the time to appeal the judgment had not yet run out. Creditinfo then entered the debt on its default register on 7 March 2019, even though the complainant had objected in time on 6 March. Persónuvernd found that the disclosure and the recording were both unlawful, because a disputed debt cannot be passed on or registered before the appeal period ends. It also held that the notice deadline had to be read in the complainant's favour. No fine was imposed, as the conditions for applying a fine were not met.

The Icelandic DPA held that the chief of police in the capital area has not complied with the Law on the processing of personal data for law enforcement purposes when requesting information and suggestions via Facebook.

Dragefossen AS, an energy company, operated a panning webcam on its office roof that live-streamed Rognan town centre on YouTube and its website, with up to 12 hours of rewind. Although faces and number plates were not legible, people could be identified from clothing, car type and other features, so personal data was processed. The company had not identified any legal basis, and the authority found none under Article 6(1)(f). It fined the company NOK 150,000 for infringing Articles 6(1) and 5(1)(a). The order to stop the surveillance was dropped because the camera had already been switched off.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of €150,000 on Xfera Móviles S.A. (defendant) for infringing Article 17, 32, 5(1)(f) GDPR and Article 21 LSSI. The fine was imposed after investigating two complaints received from the same data subject who indicated that the defendant had not stopped sending marketing messages and that the data subject was able to access third party's personal data through the 'Mi Yoigo' platform.

A lawyer complained on behalf of a member of the Pancyprian Association of Motor Vehicle Assessors that the association's letters, one to its members and one to insurance companies, linked his expulsion to alleged unlawful conduct and so disclosed his personal data. The association repeatedly failed to answer the Commissioner's requests for documents and information by the set deadlines, and it did not respond to the Commissioner's preliminary finding. The Commissioner found infringements of Articles 5(1)(a), 6(1), 9(1) and 31 GDPR. Instead of a fine, the Commissioner issued a reprimand and a warning to the association.

Following a review of 158 personal data breach notifications made by Familieretshuset between 2018 and September 2020, the Danish DPA opened an own-initiative case. Most breaches (130 of 158, about 134 in the overview) involved unintended disclosure of personal data, including protected names and addresses, largely through manual errors and faulty self-service solutions using a CPR call. The DPA issued a severe reprimand for inadequate security under Article 32(1) and for missing written data processing agreements and instructions under Article 28(3). It found Familieretshuset had complied with Article 34(1). No fine was imposed.

The Romanian DPA (ANSPDCP) imposed a fine of €500 on a natural person who held the office of Secretary-General in a subsidiary branch of a political party for publishing the personal data of 10 individuals on their website. This breached Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR.

An old locked vault containing paper files of current and former customers of Hellenic Bank was left in a Nicosia branch that the bank had leased until 2015. It stayed unattended from 2015 to 2019, when a new tenant notified the bank, which then opened the vault and moved the contents to its secure premises. The Commissioner found the bank had notified the breach late and had breached the availability of the files kept in the vault, and imposed a fine of EUR 25,000 under Articles 5(1)(e) and (f), 32(1)(b) and (c) and 33(1) GDPR. This is a listing page covering several decisions, and the Hellenic Bank entry gives no decision date or full decision text.

A complainant made a written access request under Article 15 GDPR to the Real Estate Agents Registration Council and received no reply. After the Commissioner's office asked the Council for its position and wrote to it about the apparent infringements, it again did not respond. The Commissioner ordered the Council, as controller, to comply with the access request within one month and imposed a fine of EUR 10,000 for infringements of Articles 12, 15, 31 and 58(1)(e) GDPR. The Council then complied with the order but has appealed under Article 146 of the Cypriot Constitution against the fine. This is one entry in a page that lists several Commissioner decisions from October 2020 to January 2021.

An employer asked an employee to set up automatic forwarding of their email to a shared mailbox, for operational reasons. After a complaint, the Norwegian DPA found there was no legal basis for the forwarding, in breach of the email-access regulation and the GDPR requirement of a legal basis. The enterprise also had no routines for access to email. It was ordered to improve its internal control and guidelines and to pay NOK 250,000.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of €200,000 on the energy supplier, I-DE, Redes Eléctricas Inteligentes SAU. I-DE had sent a letter to end consumers requiring them to get in touch with regards to unpaid invoices despite a contractual arrangement providing for an intermediary to communicate with end users (breach of Articles 6(1)(b), 5(1)(b) and 5(1)(c) GDPR).

The ICO held that a recruitment consultancy contravened Article 15 GDPR for failing to comply with the data subject's access request under Article 15 GDPR, as the company could not evidence its claim that the Employment Tribunal instructed them not to provide any documentation.

The Danish Data Protection Agency investigated Epic Booking, a mobile disco company, after finding close to 500,000 photos, mainly of children and young people, on its public Facebook page. The photos were taken at parties with a selfie camera. The agency found that the consent obtained was not valid (not specific, informed or freely given), that the information given to people when photographed was inadequate, and that no retention period was set. It issued serious criticism and ordered Epic Booking to delete photos published without valid consent and to set a maximum 60-day deletion period for future photos. No fine was imposed.

The ICO issued a monetary penalty notice under the Data Protection Act 1998 to Leads Work Limited, a lead generation company for Avon sales representatives. Between 16 May and 26 June 2020 the company sent about 2.67 million marketing texts to individuals whose consent, obtained through third-party data capture websites, was found not to be valid. The Commissioner found a serious contravention of regulation 22 of PECR, deliberate, and alternatively negligent, and imposed a penalty of £250,000, reducible by 20% for early payment. The notice also records a breach of regulation 23 of PECR, which the company accepted.

The Icelandic DPA ruled in a case regarding the use of audio and video recording equipment in police cars by the police in the capital area in 2017 and 2018. The decision finds that the complainant's right to information, including the police's obligation to provide information, was respected in 2017 but not in 2018.

After a complaint about a private gymnasium's requirements for online tests, including a mandatory external camera, full-room recording and a face-detection indicator, the Slovenian supervisory authority opened an inspection. The school said it had adopted rules for online tests but had not started written online assessments, and it stopped the face-detection practice after being told of the authority's concerns. The authority therefore discontinued the proceedings without a fine. The decision is an order (sklep) to stop the procedure, not a finding of violation.

The Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEDP) imposed a warning sanction on a local council for using a biometric control system to monitor the working hours of employees without having informed them in accordance with Article 13 GDPR.
The Italian DPA (Garante per la protezione dei dati personali) imposed a fine of €300,000 on the national social security institute (INPS) for violating Articles 5(1)(a)(c)(d), 2, 25 and 35 GDPR.

A former employee of the Comune di Conflenti complained that a municipal council resolution published on the online notice board (Albo Pretorio) named her and contained employment information, including an extract of her resignation letter. The Garante found the publication unlawful: there was no valid legal basis for disseminating the data, the data were minimised incorrectly, and the resolution stayed online beyond the period set by the transparency rules. The municipality was fined EUR 2,000, which the Garante said was effective, proportionate and dissuasive. The Garante also ordered publication of the decision on its website, but no further corrective measures, because the municipality had removed the data and the processing had ended.

A former employee complained that a small municipality published on its online notice board a decision accepting his resignation. It included assessments of his work and information on his sick leave, identifying him by initials. The mayor also gave the press details that appeared in a newspaper. The Garante found no legal basis for the publication, and health data may never be disseminated. It fined the municipality EUR 6,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

On 25 October 2019 the website repubblica.it, linked to Gedi, published images of two people detained over a serious crime, shown visibly physically restrained (handcuffs only pixelated). The Garante urgently restricted further dissemination, but Gedi neither replied nor removed the images until 25 February 2020, and similar images were still online on 18 February 2021. The Garante found the publication unlawful and contrary to Article 5(1)(a) GDPR, the Italian Code and the journalists' code of ethics, and found non-compliance with its order and its information request. It banned further processing of such images, fined Gedi EUR 20,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A parent complained that the Regional School Office for Lazio, answering a request from the Public Administration Department about alleged irregularities in the allocation of support teaching hours, sent documents containing his child's personal and health data, including a diagnostic code. The Garante found that the disclosure was not necessary to answer the Department and had no suitable legal basis, so it breached Articles 5(1)(a), 6 and 9 GDPR and Articles 2-ter and 2-sexies of the Italian Code. It fined the office EUR 4,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

A university hospital in Florence notified a personal data breach: paper health documentation (an emergency room lab report) of one patient was handed to another person, caused by a doctor picking up a printout left in a shared printer tray. The Garante found unlawful communication of health data in breach of Articles 5 and 9 GDPR. It considered no further corrective measures necessary because the conduct had ceased and improvements were made, but imposed a fine of EUR 6,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine on Avilon Center SL for making a commercial call to a individual registered on the Robinson List in breach of Article 48(1)(b) LGT and Article 21 GDPR in conjunction with Article 23(4) LOPDGDD. Avilon Center SL made an voluntary, early and guilty payment of €12,000.

The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) changes the language of the procedure against IAB to Dutch after its interlocutory decision 01/2021 (setting French as the procedural language) was appealed in front of the Court of Markets. The parties can still speak or write in Dutch, French and English.

A woman repeatedly received unsolicited marketing SMS messages from a company even after she objected by email on 3 and 4 August 2020 and asked for erasure. The company replied that it held no data on her but kept texting her, including after the Office warned it in September 2020 and did not respond. The Office found a breach of the right to erasure under Art. 17(1)(c) GDPR following an objection to direct marketing under Art. 21(2), and by penalty order imposed a fine of CZK 30,000. The company could file an objection within 8 days.

A minor, represented by her legal guardian, complained that the City of Vienna gave an incomplete access response (Art. 15 GDPR) about her hospital medical records from 2019. The authority held that the controller had breached the right of access by providing incomplete information on her health data, and ordered it to provide complete information within four weeks. The guardian's requests for a declaration that demanding an ID copy was unlawful, and that a registration certificate could reasonably have been obtained by the controller itself, were dismissed. No fine is stated in the text.

The Croatian DPA (AZOP) found that the leading security company in Croatia, acting as a data processor, enabled the data breach by not maintaining adequate and sufficient technical and organizational measures for personal data security for more than two and a half years.

The Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) imposed a warning sanction on a private individual for the installation of a video surveillance system without informing the subjects who may be recorded of the data processing, in violation of Article 13 and Article 5 (1) (c) GDPR.

The Belgian DPA's Litigation Chamber examined smart cameras used by the tourism body Westtoer to count passers-by on the Belgian coast during the Covid-19 pandemic, operated by a processor under a public tender. The Chamber found the camera system itself lawful in its principles, necessity and data protection by design, with no violation of Articles 5(1)(a)-(c) or 25. It found violations of transparency rules (Articles 12 and 13), cookie consent (Articles 6(1)(a), 7(1) and 7(3)), the record of processing (Article 30) and the DPO's reporting line (Article 38(3)). Because the controller had cooperated and updated its privacy statement, it received a reprimand and orders rather than a fine.

The UK Information Commissioner issued a monetary penalty notice against Valca, a lead-generation company, for sending unsolicited marketing text messages without valid consent. The messages relied on indirect consent from a privacy policy listing about 450 companies, and the first messages had no opt-out link. The Commissioner found breaches of regulations 22 and 23 of PECR, treated them as deliberate or negligent, and set a penalty of £80,000. The notice is under the Data Protection Act 1998 and PECR, not the GDPR.
The Finnish DPA ordered Suomen Asiakastieto Oy to remove a payment default entry from their credit information registry which no longer had a legal basis to be be retained.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) sanctioned a city hall for not satisfying a data subject's access request to his personal data concerning the payment of local taxes.

A customer complained that a sports retailer sent him promotional SMS messages after he had objected by email to receiving marketing. The company said his number had been deleted, but a second promotional SMS arrived in November 2019 because of an employee's error. The Authority found that the company did not honour the erasure/objection request and had no effective deletion procedures in practice. It fined the company EUR 20,000 for breaching Articles 17, 21 and 12(3) and Article 25(1) GDPR.

A patient of a primary care centre run by the controller took a voluntary PCR test for SARS-CoV-2 on 28 September 2020 and received a text message that his result was negative. The controller then forwarded the negative result to the district administrative authority (Bezirksverwaltungsbehörde), and the complainant argued this breached his right to confidentiality. The DSB held that a negative test is health data under Art. 4(15) GDPR, but that the disclosure was lawful because the Epidemic Act (EpiG) and a health ministry regulation, extended during COVID-19 to cover negative results, created a legal obligation under Art. 9(2)(i) and Art. 6(1)(c) GDPR. The complaint was dismissed.

Telenet, a telecoms and TV provider, was referred to the GBA's inspection service after a customer's complaint about finding the opt-out from direct marketing, and after data breach notifications. The Litigation Chamber found that, until March 2019, Telenet had no consolidated way to object to all direct marketing at once, which breached Article 21(2) read with 12(2) and merited a reprimand. It found limited breaches of the transparency and information duties (Articles 12(1), 12(2), 13 and 14) but imposed no sanction for them. It imposed no fine and dismissed the other complaints, with recommendations.

The Spanish AEPD closed procedure PS/00430/2020 against Vodafone España after the company paid a fine. A data subject who had asked for deletion and had already obtained two earlier sanctions for the same conduct kept receiving invoice-availability emails from Vodafone in 2020. The initiation agreement proposed EUR 200,000 for a presumed breach of Article 6(1) GDPR. Two 20% reductions (acknowledgement of responsibility and voluntary payment) brought it to EUR 120,000, which the company paid on 2 February 2021. The resolution terminates the procedure.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of €2,000 against Ripobruna 207, S.L. (defendant) for the alleged violation of Article 5(1)(c) GDPR for the unauthorised use of two video surveillance cameras that also recorded parts of the public road without any justified cause. The original fine of €2,000 was reduced for voluntary payment to €1,600.

The Austrian DSB fined a small company, A*** GmbH, EUR 3,000 for failing to respond to its requests for a statement in three complaint proceedings. Three employees had complained that the company shared their sick-leave health data in a WhatsApp group. The company did not respond at all in two cases and responded only after the deadline in the third. The DSB found a breach of Article 31 GDPR, sanctioned under Article 83(4)(a), and found negligence rather than intent. The penalty is stated to be final.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) found that the data processor, Vamavi Phone SL, had violated Article 48(1) LGT, Article 21 GDPR in link with Article 23 LOPDGDD and Article 28 GDPR by making a commercial call on behalf of Vodafone España, SAU to a data subject registered on the Robinson List. Vamavi paid a fine of €24,000 (reduced from €40,000).

The National School of Judiciary and Public Prosecution notified a personal data breach after a copy of its training platform user database, created during a test migration in February 2020, was posted publicly online in April 2020. The data of about 50,000 judicial staff and others was affected. The Polish DPA found that the School had not applied adequate security measures, had not tested their effectiveness during the migration, and had entrusted processing to a hosting company under a processing agreement that did not meet Article 28(3). It imposed the statutory maximum fine of PLN 100,000 on the School and discontinued the proceedings in all other respects, including those against the processor for the remaining alleged breaches.

After press reports, the Italian DPA investigated the Ministry of Economic Development, which had published online a list of over 5,000 'qualified managers' with names, tax codes, emails and full CVs, freely downloadable. The Garante found the publication lacked a suitable legal basis, since a directorial decree is not a regulation and was not provided for by the primary law. It also found the Ministry appointed its data protection officer and notified the contact details late. The Garante fined the Ministry EUR 75,000, ordered publication of the decision and noted it in its internal register.

A hospital foundation notified a personal data breach: because two patients had the same name, a postal package containing one patient's medical report was sent to a homonymous third party. The Garante found this was a disclosure of health data without a legal basis, breaching the lawfulness and confidentiality principles and Article 9. No further corrective measures were needed because the foundation had already contacted the patients, sent the correct documents and reviewed its processes. It imposed a fine of EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

Permits for limited traffic zones (ZTL) in Rome carried a QR code that anyone could read with a generic mobile app, giving access to the names of permit holders and users and vehicle plates. By changing a numeric parameter in the verification web address, other permits could be viewed without any authentication. The Garante found breaches of the basic principles, the lack of a legal basis, the absence of a processor contract with the hosting provider Atac, and inadequate security. It fined Roma Capitale EUR 350,000, ordered corrective authentication measures within 30 days and ordered publication of the decision.

Roma Servizi, processor for Roma Capitale, issued paper ZTL (limited traffic zone) permits with QR codes that anyone could decode with a generic app to reach the permit holder's and user's personal data. The online verification service had no authentication, and changing a numeric ID in the URL exposed other permits. The Garante found a breach of Article 32 GDPR, fined the company EUR 60,000, ordered stronger authentication (password quality, brute-force protection) within 30 days, and ordered publication of the decision.

A hospital group notified a personal data breach after a patient found, in the digital copy of her own medical record, lab reports belonging to 7 other patients. The Garante found the processing unlawful, in breach of the principles of lawfulness and integrity/confidentiality, Article 9 and Article 32 GDPR, and Article 75 of the Italian Code. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased and the documents were returned. It fined the hospital EUR 45,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

The Romanian authority investigated ING Bank N.V. Amsterdam's Bucharest branch after the bank notified a personal data security breach. The bank had sent files on two different dates to a contractual partner, through an intermediary company, for issuing insurance policies. The files contained outdated information because the policy monitoring staff did not check and process the policies under the internal working procedure, affecting 270 individuals. The authority found the technical and organisational measures in place before the incident insufficient and fined the bank.

IMY investigated the Swedish Police Authority after media reports that police staff had used the Clearview AI facial recognition app. Employees in the National Operations Department and region South used it from autumn 2019 to 3 March 2020, uploading images that were turned into biometric data. IMY found the Police had not taken adequate organisational measures, had processed biometric data without showing it was absolutely necessary, and had not carried out a data protection impact assessment. It imposed an administrative fine of SEK 2,500,000 and ordered training and organisational measures, informing the data subjects concerned, and deletion of the data entered into Clearview AI, all by 15 September 2021.
The Slovenian DPA decided that car registration plates may be personal data.

A former employee complained that his employer's answer to his subject access request (after he had been reinstated following a dispute) was unsatisfactory. The employer refused to give him a copy of certain emails and IT logs, and the Chambre Contentieuse accepted that refusal on the ground of the employer's business secrecy. The Chambre found that the employer violated Articles 15(1) and 15(3) GDPR by refusing access to and a copy of HR file annotations, which the employer had erased after the request. It ordered a sworn statement confirming the erasure and an order to bring the processing of HR annotations into compliance with Article 15, but imposed neither a fine nor a reprimand, citing the company's size, its lack of prior sanctions and its efforts on security and data protection.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of €5,000 on Predase Servicios Integrales SL for infringing Article 13 GDPR. PSI did not have a privacy policy, nor any information on processing in the contact section of its webpage (which required the provision of personal data).

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of €5,000 on the owner of a property that he rented out. The defendant had placed a video camera inside the rented property which went beyond filming the entrance as he claimed. This breached Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.

A complainant objected that a company specialised in kindergarten and school photography printed small black-and-white images of her children on the invoices it sends to debt collectors, and on the invoices' packing lists. The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman found that the controller had not complied with the data minimisation principle in Article 5(1)(c) or with data protection by default in Article 25(2). The controller was ordered under Article 58(2)(d) to bring its processing into line so that invoices no longer show unnecessary personal data. No fine was imposed, and the decision is final.

The Dutch DPA fined an unnamed orthodontic practice €12,000 for failing to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to secure personal data, including that belonging to children, on its website.

A complainant objected to Sjúkratryggingar Íslands requiring copies of her flight tickets when she applied for reimbursement of medical costs incurred abroad. The authority accepted that the agency relies on a public-authority basis to verify the length of stay abroad, and that the request did not breach the general data protection principles. The complaint was therefore not upheld and the collection was found lawful.

A former employee complained that Cyberbook AS had switched on automatic forwarding of their personal mailbox at the company. The forwarding went on for several months and the person was never told. The Norwegian Data Protection Authority found that this broke the regulations on employers' access to email, and also the GDPR requirements on legal basis, information, handling the employee's objection, and deletion. It ordered the company to set up written routines for access to current and former employees' mailboxes and to pay a NOK 200,000 fine.

A customer asked Iberdrola Clientes in November 2016 to cancel her personal data and gave a new notification address after moving out of the supplied property. Iberdrola kept sending payment demands to the old supply address, where the letters were returned, and her data were reported to the ASNEF debtor file. Iberdrola also kept using the old address after it had been told of the change, and did not act on the cancellation request.
