The AEPD fined the company EUR 50,000 for breaching the accuracy principle in Article 5(1)(d) GDPR and EUR 50,000 for breaching Article 17 GDPR, a total of EUR 100,000.

A transport company (the controller) asked the Austrian DSB for prior consultation under Art. 36 GDPR on a planned video-based 'impact detection' system for railway bridges, after its own data protection impact assessment left a high residual risk. The DSB found that the planned measures (triggered recording, short ring-buffer storage, access limits, signage and a legitimate-interest assessment) sufficiently contain the risk, so there is no high risk. The application for prior consultation was therefore dismissed. No fine was imposed.

A property investor complained that Bergens Tidende had obtained his credit information and published it in a 2019 article about a bankruptcy petition, and that some of the published information was wrong. On 18 February 2020 Datatilsynet held that the newspaper's collection and publication were solely for journalistic purposes and so fell under the journalism exemption in Norway's Personopplysningsloven § 3, which implements GDPR Article 85. On 2 February 2021 the Privacy Appeals Board upheld that decision, finding that no balancing of interests applies to core journalism of this kind, whether or not the published information was accurate.

A data subject twice asked an auction company (31 March and 2 July 2020) to delete a public auction notice PDF containing his name, date of birth and address from its indexable website. The company did not respond, even after the Office's warning of 29 July 2020, and the notice was still online on 29 October 2020. The company argued the publication was required by the public auctions act and that it had removed the notice after the penalty order. The Office found a breach of the right to erasure under Article 17(1)(a) GDPR and fined the company CZK 10,000 plus CZK 1,000 costs.

A customer objected by email on 29 June 2020 to the processing of his data and asked for erasure, but the company still sent him marketing SMS messages on 19 August and 25 November 2020, even after the authority had warned it. The company blamed an individual employee's error and admitted the offence. The authority found a breach of the right to erasure under Article 17(1)(c) GDPR and fined it CZK 2,000, plus CZK 1,000 in procedural costs. An earlier penalty order of CZK 20,000 had been cancelled after the company objected.

The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) held that intent is not a criterium to assess processing and that mistakenly sending an e-mail does not necessarily constitute a data breach as a human error does not always mean the technical and organisational measures are not adequate. Finally, the DPA held that merely receiving an e-mail is not processing.

A lawyer complained on behalf of an individual that the National Police Commissioner refused his request for information on which staff had looked up his data in the police case system (LÖKE) under a specified case number, and that the request took too long. Persónuvernd found the refusal to name the staff members lawful, but found the refusal to disclose which other controllers had looked up his data under that case number unlawful, and ordered the Commissioner to provide that information. It found the processing time compliant with the rules.

Roma Capitale published in full, on its online official notice board, a school canteen debt notice containing personal data of a 9-year-old child and the mother. It did so to notify a homeless person with a conventional address, relying on a city executive resolution. The Garante found a breach of lawfulness and minimisation principles and the lack of a proper legal basis for online dissemination, since a municipal resolution is not a law or regulation. It fined the city EUR 10,000 and ordered it to bring notifications to homeless residents into line with state law, which never provides for publishing the whole act.

A mother complained that a company distributing gift packs to (expectant) mothers passed on her data to third-party partners for direct marketing, and that she was still contacted after objecting. After an Inspection Service investigation, the Litigation Chamber found that the company breached the GDPR on principles, lawful basis and consent, information, accountability, data protection by design and processor arrangements. It ordered the company to bring its processing into line within six months and imposed a fine of EUR 50,000. The Chamber refused to reduce the fine despite the company's COVID-19 financial difficulties, and decided to publish the decision with the company's identity.

A hospital nurse in the gynaecology ward of a Romagna health authority hospital phoned a patient after discharge using an old number from the records, not the one the patient had given for this stay, and spoke to the patient's husband, revealing the ward. The patient had expressly refused to let third parties know about her health, and had undergone a voluntary termination of pregnancy. The Garante found that the authority's technical and organisational measures were inadequate and that the processing breached Articles 5(1)(a), (d), (f), 9 and 32(1)(b) GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 50,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no further corrective measures since the conduct had ceased and the authority had put new measures in place.

A university hospital in Siena notified a personal data breach: because of an enveloping error, a medical report from a genetic consultation, containing health and sex life data of two people, was posted to unrelated third parties. The Garante found unlawful processing in breach of Articles 5(1)(f) and 9 GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no corrective measures because the conduct had ceased and the document was recovered. The Garante weighed the isolated, unintentional nature of the error, the small number of people affected and the hospital's cooperation.

A university hospital in Parma notified the Garante of two data breaches in which medical records handed to a patient's parents and to a deceased patient's heir contained test reports belonging to other patients. The Garante merged the proceedings and found that placing other patients' health data in the records disclosed it to unauthorised persons without a legal basis, breaching Articles 5(1)(f) and 9 GDPR. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased and the hospital had taken remedial steps. It imposed a single fine of EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

Two data subjects complained that Barclays Bank Plc kept negative credit information about their settled loan in the Crif credit information system for 36 months after a settlement agreement, when they asked for deletion. The bank argued the longer retention period applied because of the loss it had suffered, but admitted it was a good-faith error and that the correct period was 24 months. The Garante found breaches of the principles of lawfulness and storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(a) and (e)), and issued a reprimand because the case was a minor violation. No corrective order was made on the deletion request, because the data had already been deleted during the proceedings.

The Danish Data Protection Agency examined, on its own initiative after a telephone enquiry, how the IT University of Copenhagen used the ProctorExam monitoring tool for an online exam in Algorithms and Data Structures in May 2020. The tool recorded video, audio, screen and browser history during the three-hour exam for about 330 students. The Agency found that the processing was within the GDPR rules on principles, lawful basis, security and impact assessment, and it issued no criticism. It did make recommendations, for example on clearer information to students and on browser settings, but these are not binding orders.

The ICO issued Rancom Security Limited, a home security firm, with a monetary penalty for making unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered with the TPS, in breach of regulation 21 of PECR. The calls were made between June 2017 and May 2018 and led to 94 complaints. The Commissioner found the contravention serious and negligent, and imposed a penalty of £110,000, with a 20% early-payment discount to £88,000. No enforcement notice was issued because Rancom said it had stopped marketing calls.

A job applicant complained that Landsnet hf. kept his personal data from his unsuccessful job application after the recruitment ended, and refused his request for deletion. Landsnet said it is obliged under the Icelandic Public Archives Act (No. 77/2014) to keep its records and cannot destroy them. The authority dismissed the part of the complaint about the refusal of the deletion request, because it could not decide whether the oral request was made. It found that the retention was lawful under Article 6(1)(c) GDPR and did not breach the basic principles of Article 5 GDPR, so no violation was found.

A prepaid mobile customer complained that his phone number was assigned to a third party for four days, his SIM card was deactivated, and the third party could have accessed his calls and linked accounts. The Litigation Chamber found that the provider had not taken enough precautions in identifying and verifying prepaid customers, and had not notified the breach to the authority or the data subject. It imposed a EUR 25,000 fine and ordered the provider to bring its processing into compliance within three months. A note at the top states the decision was later repealed by decision 61/2021 of 19 May 2021.

The Italian DPA opened formal proceedings against TikTok with a note of 15 December 2020, alleging breaches of several GDPR provisions and finding serious weaknesses, above all in how the platform checks the age of its users. TikTok asked for more time and the deadline for its reply was extended to 29 January 2021. In the meantime press reports linked the death of a 10-year-old girl to imitative practices connected with her use of the platform. On 22 January 2021 TikTok had not yet replied, and the Garante's preliminary examination showed serious shortcomings in its age checks. The Garante used Articles 58(2)(f) and 66(1) GDPR to order a provisional limitation: TikTok must stop processing the data of users in Italy whose age is not certain. It took effect immediately and was to last until the reply could be examined, a date then set at 15 February 2021, subject to further review. This is a provisional measure: no fine, and it does not decide whether TikTok breached the GDPR.

A complainant asked MAG Interactive AB in May 2019 to erase their account data, and the company deleted the data within 16 days. The company did not inform the complainant of the outcome until 6 November 2020, which was due to an oversight. IMY found that the company infringed Article 12(3) GDPR by not informing the data subject of the measures taken within one month. IMY closed the case without corrective measures, taking into account the circumstances and the improvements the company said it would make.

The applicant had bought glasses from the controller's optician shop in 2014. Despite asking three times (7.3.2018, 19.11.2018, 22.11.2018) to be removed and to stop marketing, the applicant received direct marketing in November 2018 and again in November 2019, which the controller blamed on technical errors. The controller refused erasure because it must retain patient records under health-care law. The Data Protection Ombudsman found that the controller failed to give effect to the objection to direct marketing (Art. 21(2) and (3)), failed to take adequate measures under Art. 25(2), and gave no reasons for refusing the first two requests (Art. 12(4)). The erasure request was rejected under Art. 17(3)(b), and a reprimand was issued. No fine was imposed.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a fine of €50,000 on Alterna Operador Integral SL (Flip Energy) for processing a data subject's personal data without a legal basis (Article 6(1) GDPR). Flip Energy had switched switched the data subject over from the energy provider Naturgy to Flip Energy without obtaining consent or a contract for doing so.

The complainant held several mobile lines with the controller, one used by her son. Third parties impersonating her had the ownership of one line transferred to a third party without any identity check, and a replacement SIM was then issued in a shop. The controller admitted the data had been misused but argued that the fault lay with the impersonator and that its verification procedure was adequate. The AEPD rejected this, finding no proof of the diligence required by the lawfulness principle, and imposed a fine of EUR 75,000 for infringing Article 6(1) GDPR.

The controller sent unsolicited offers through the Czech data box system to 4,238 natural persons between 2 November and 3 December 2020, without any legal basis and without giving the information required by Article 14. The Office found two offences (breach of Article 6(1) and of Article 14 GDPR). Following the accused's objection to an earlier penalty order, which was cancelled, it imposed a single fine of CZK 285,000 under the absorption principle, plus CZK 1,000 costs. Aggravating factors were the abuse of data boxes during the state of emergency, the large number of people affected and the multiple breaches.

The controller sent unsolicited offers through the Czech data-box system to 23,302 natural persons between 2 November and 3 December 2020, during a state of emergency when data-box messages were free. It had no legal basis under Article 6(1) and did not give the Article 14 information. The Office found two offences and, applying the absorption principle, imposed a single fine of CZK 666,000 plus CZK 1,000 costs. The earlier penalty order was cancelled after the controller objected, and the controller made no statement in the proceedings.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a €2000 fine on The Washpoint SL for failing to provide a Privacy Policy on their website (Article 13 GDPR) and for the absence of a reject button on the second layer of their Cookie Policy (Article 22(2) LSSI).

The Czech DPA issued a penalty order against a company that acts as controller for the owners of flats in an apartment building. A data subject had repeatedly asked it for information on the processing of his personal data and received no reply, even after the authority drew the company's attention to the duty. The authority found a breach of the right of access under Article 15(1) GDPR and imposed a fine of CZK 30,000. The company could lodge an objection within 8 days, which would cancel the order and continue the proceedings.

A person who applied to become a volunteer support person for children complained that the City of Helsinki had obtained police records about him, including reports where he was the injured party, through a consent form. The Data Protection Ombudsman found that the city had no proper legal basis for obtaining and processing such police data beyond a criminal record extract, that the consent was not valid, and that the data subject had not been properly informed. The office issued a reprimand and ordered the city to bring its processing into compliance within 30 days. No fine was imposed.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) held that a consumers and users association (ASOCAPAC) breached Article 22(2) LSSI. The first layer of the cookie banner and the cookie policy on their website did not contain sufficient information and a "refuse all cookies" option was missing.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) imposed a €1000 fine on a beauty salon for breaching Article 17 GDPR and Article 21 LSSI. The salon sent a marketing SMS to a client months after confirming that they had deleted the client's personal data.

The Latvian DPA (Datu valsts inspekcija) imposed a fine of €65,000 on SIA “Lursoft IT" for breaching Articles 5(1)(a), (b), (c) and 6(1) GDPR. Lursoft published personal data from the "Insolvency Register" as well as personal data that is to be submitted to the "Register of Enterprises" on its website.

ARPAC, a regional environmental agency, notified the Garante of the theft of an external hard disk from its offices. The disk held identity documents, tax documents, payslips and refund files and was connected to a server in a room any employee could enter. The backup had failed, so most data was permanently lost. The Garante found that ARPAC had no adequate security measures (no working backup or restoration, no pseudonymisation or encryption, no regular testing). It fined ARPAC EUR 8,000 for breaching Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 and ordered publication of the decision.

A data subject asked the clinic on 19 September 2019 for access under Article 15 to her own data and to data about her two minor daughters. The clinic answered only after the Garante's office intervened, 62 days after the request. The clinic blamed a hardware failure that led to a PC replacement. The Garante found a breach of Article 12(3) in relation to Article 15, treated the delay as negligent rather than intentional, noted the clinic's cooperation and lack of relevant prior breaches, and imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 with publication of the decision on its website.

The Bologna health authority notified a personal data breach: because of a manual error by a technician of its supplier, hospital discharge letters with therapies of oncology patients were wrongly loaded into 182 electronic health records (49 active). Only 14 holders opened their record in the period, and two patients certainly saw other people's documents. The documents were deleted after about six hours. The Garante found a breach of Articles 5(1)(f) and 9 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 18,000, plus publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased.

The Italian DPA investigated Regione Lazio's regional health-booking call centre service (ReCUP), run by an external cooperative. The Region never validly appointed the cooperative as data processor; the earlier appointments were found to have no effect, and a proper Article 28 appointment was only made in January 2019. The Garante found the processing unlawful from 1999 to January 2019, in breach of Articles 5(2)(a) and 28 GDPR. It fined the Region EUR 75,000 and ordered publication of the decision, but adopted no corrective measures since the conduct had ended.

A school sent a newsletter to the parents of all its pupils with every recipient's email address visible, because the addresses were put in CC instead of BCC. The complainant, one of those parents, complained. The Litigation Chamber found that the school had no lawful basis for disclosing the complainant's address to other parents, that this was incompatible further processing, and that the school's policies and measures under Articles 24 and 25 were not applied in practice. It issued a reprimand and ordered the school to bring its processing into compliance within three months. No fine was imposed.
The Spanish DPA (AEDP) accepted a complaint against 'Associació Catalana per la Participació Política' as the organisation failed to respond to a citizen's request for suppression (Article 17 GDPR).

The French DPA (CNIL) ordered the Ministry of Interior to cease the use of drones equipped with cameras by police forces. The Ministry violated its obligations to process personal data only where authorised by a specific legal provision and to conduct a privacy impact assessment.

A complaint was lodged in Germany, then transferred to the Cyprus authority as lead authority, about a cruise-ship crew recruitment company. The company required employees to sign a general 'Authorisation for release of medical records' before boarding, and the authority treated that consent as invalid because employees had no real choice. The authority found that consent is not a valid basis in this employment context and that the company must collect only data that is necessary. It ordered the company to stop processing employees' health data on the basis of consent and to bring processing into line with the GDPR, reporting back within one month. No fine was imposed.

A performing artist complained that a company and its manager ran a Facebook fan page carrying her full name without her consent, and ignored her requests to hand over control and to stop. After an earlier interim decision (14/2020) that was not complied with, the Litigation Chamber examined the case on the merits. It dismissed the complaint against the manager, who was not a controller, and warned the company on data portability, a request that had become moot because Facebook transferred the admin rights to the complainant. It found the company had no lawful basis for the processing (Art. 6(1)) and failed to act on the objection and communicate properly (Art. 21(1) with 12(3)), and fined it EUR 10,000.
The Polish DPA (Urząd Ochrony Danych Osobowych) imposed an administrative fine of over PLN 136,000 (approx. €30,000) on an energy sector company for failing to report a data protection breach.

The company reported a ransomware attack in April 2020 that encrypted about 80,000 records, including health data, and was not notified to data subjects. The President of UODO found that the company used operating systems and a database system whose vendor support had ended, and that its internal testing of security measures was not regular or documented. The company was found to have infringed Article 5(1)(f), 24(1), 25(1) and 32(1) and (2) GDPR, and was given a reprimand (upomnienie) rather than a fine, citing the one-off nature of the event and the remedial steps taken.

The Belgian DPA (APD/GBA) decided, in an interlocutory decision, on the language to be used in a procedure concerning GDPR complaints filed by complainants in various Member States against IAB Europe. The DPA chose French, as English is not a national language in Belgium and the defendant, who does not speak Dutch, requested French as the procedural language.

The Lower Saxony data protection authority fined notebooksbilliger.de AG EUR 10.4 million for video surveillance of its employees over at least two years without a legal basis. Cameras covered workplaces, sales rooms, warehouses and break areas, and some also covered customer seating areas. Recordings were often kept for 60 days, longer than necessary. The company has since made its video surveillance lawful. The fine was not yet final at the time of the press release.

A window-fitting-hardware manufacturer sent a customer a letter in January 2020 about possibly faulty fittings, having obtained her name and address from the window seller. The complainant said the company had processed her data for about five months without informing her and that the letter did not meet Article 14 GDPR. The Austrian DSB held that the company breached its information duty by not stating the legal basis for processing, and ordered it to provide that information within four weeks. The other complaints (timing, other Article 14 content, and language) were dismissed, as the information was given during the proceedings and the German-language procedure was considered sufficient.

A public medical university posted recordings of practical paediatric exams on an e-learning platform, which showed students presenting student cards and ID cards. The university did not report the breach to the President of UODO or notify the affected students, judging the risk low. The President found a high risk, held that Art. 33(1) and Art. 34(1) GDPR were breached, ordered the students to be notified within 3 days of the decision becoming final, and imposed a fine of PLN 25,000.

A former employee of a medical business copied the personal data of 100 patients to market his own services, and the business notified the breach to UODO but chose not to inform the patients despite rating the risk as high. UODO ordered it in February 2020 to notify the patients with the content required by Article 34(2). The business sent incomplete notices and failed to prove it had complied, and ignored guidance from UODO staff. UODO therefore fined it PLN 85,588 (the equivalent of EUR 20,000) under Article 83(6) for not complying with a corrective order.

The Polish DPA imposed a fine of €5000 on a company for failing to comply with the obligation to cooperate with the supervisory authority and not providing it with all information necessary to fulfil its tasks in the course of the proceedings.
